full_text:
MdM network welcomes the European commission communication on humanitarian action as an important political sign that humanitarian aid remains a strategic priority for the European Union but warns against shortcomings and calls for concrete implementation and predictable financing.

The European Commission adopted today its 
Communication on EU Humanitarian Action, a significant policy framework document intended to guide the EU’s approach to humanitarian engagement over the coming years.

Médecins du Monde – Doctors of the World welcomes the European Commission’s Humanitarian Communication as an important policial signal that humanitarian aid remains a strategic priority for the European Union
 at a time of erosion of respect for international humanitarian law, shrinking funds and humanitarian space, and rising conflicts and fragility.

One of the most substantive contributions of the Communication is its 
clear definitional framing of humanitarian diplomacy
 and its unambiguous emphasis on International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and the protection of humanitarian workers. In a period marked by alarming rates of attacks on aid workers and deliberate obstruction of humanitarian access, this political reaffirmation is most welcomed.

The Communication includes a notably 
strong commitment to Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR)
 in humanitarian settings — an area that has been subject to significant political pressure globally, including from the current US administration. The introduction of the 
SHIELD initiative
 (Sexual and Reproductive Health in Emergencies and Life in Dignity) is a concrete and welcome development.

We also welcome the reaffirmation of 
EU engagement in fragile and conflict-affected settings. Additionally, references to simplified reporting requirements are welcomed. Bureaucratic reporting burdens have been a persistent barrier for NGOs and any steps toward streamlining these processes improve humanitarian effectiveness.

The emphasis on 
pooled funds
 and the conditionality attached to compliance with humanitarian principles is positive though implementation will be key. Country-Based Pooled Funds should be treated as one modality among others, alongside bilateral and multi-year funding, to ensure flexibility and sustainability. As the EU deepens its engagement with pooled mechanisms, it must ensure that governance, partner selection and design processes remain transparent, principled and free from political conditionalities that could compromise humanitarian independence.

However, the question of 
disinformation
 and harmful narratives, which constitutes a growing threat to the humanitarian space, remains underdeveloped. The coverage is fragmented and lacks a coherent framework for how the EU intends to respond to coordinated disinformation campaigns targeting humanitarian actors. Section 3.2 also references disinformation in the domestic EU context, including engagement with EU citizens through communication campaigns. While welcome, the domestic framing should not come at the expense of a more robust treatment of disinformation in field contexts, given the growing weaponisation of disinformation in conflict settings.

Several provisions merit careful scrutiny. The emphasis on 
private sector investment, including artificial intelligence, as a 
“funding and efficiency driver”
 (p.13) reflects a broader trend in EU policy toward competitiveness, including in the humanitarian space. While certain private sector partnerships can bring added value in specific contexts (e.g., logistics, supply chains), the framing risks normalising a transactional approach to humanitarian action that prioritises cost-efficiency over principled response in sector that are not intended to generate profit by nature. The use of AI in humanitarian operations (e.g., data analysis, needs assessments), raises serious questions regarding 
accountability, data protection, and the concentration of technological power
 in a small number of private actors, therefore the translation of this into programming should be under great scrutiny.

In addition, any EU data-sharing framework among humanitarian partners should require robust safeguards and be built on a strong governance and accountability system, 
meaningful consent, data protection principles, and robust protection against misuse. In contexts where humanitarian data can be accessed by state security actors or used for population surveillance, the risks of data-sharing are substantial. Finally, the proposed EU-wide certification framework for humanitarian organisations risks creating bureaucratic gatekeeping that disadvantage smaller and local actors.

Political ambition must now be matched with concrete implementation and predictable financing. The Communication’s value depends entirely on whether it is backed by robust and sustained funding.

As an immediate step, the Communication should be backed by 
Council Conclusion
s to ensure Member State ownership and political accountability.

On financing, the negotiations on the next Multiannual Financial Framework, particularly the Global Europe Instrument, will be the true test of the EU’s humanitarian ambition. Médecins du Monde calls for:

A humanitarian envelope of at least 25 billion euros under the next MFF

At least 20% of the GEI dedicated to non-programmable actions, preserving flexibility to respond to sudden-onset crises

The Emergencies cushion to be ring-fenced and protected from reallocation to other policy priorities, including migration management

Multi-year, predictable funding commitments that allow humanitarian organisations to plan and deliver effectively

related.summary: In a directive issued by the Taliban’s military courts and reviewed by the Guardian, the ban was to take effect this week and prohibits “high rank, low rank, general mujahideen, or service staff” from using mobile phones. “The private sector was freaking out, the banking sector was freaking out, even their own people – the security sector and the supreme leader’s office – and they realised ‘OK guys, we didn’t really think this through’, so they put it back on,” the analyst said.
bullets: In a directive issued by the Taliban’s military courts and reviewed by the Guardian, the ban was to take effect this week and prohibits “high rank, low rank, general mujahideen, or service staff” from using mobile phones.

“The private sector was freaking out, the banking sector was freaking out, even their own people – the security sector and the supreme leader’s office – and they realised ‘OK guys, we didn’t really think this through’, so they put it back on,” the analyst said.

Video appears to show Taliban officials smashing up smartphones after ban announced Reports and sources inside Afghanistan say that the bans are being implemented in an “ad-hoc” way – in some areas targeting only government officials, in some cities and provinces extending to women, civilians, medical workers, schoolteachers and students.
But also, it could be a prelude to a blanket ban and they are just testing the waters,” said an analyst who works on Afghanistan.
In September, authorities ordered an internet blackout which lasted two days and was vaguely justified by concerns over pornography; the order said the cutoff was to “prevent immorality”.
related.excerpt: The Taliban have ordered a sweeping ban on the use of smartphones by government officials – in what some analysts say could foreshadow broader, population-level restrictions. In a directive issued by the Taliban’s military courts and reviewed by the Guardian, the ban was to take effect this week and prohibits “high rank, low rank, general mujahideen, or service staff” from using mobile phones. In one video published online, a Taliban official appears to be shown reading the banning order from his phone while the other person is shown breaking phones. The order states: “If anyone uses one, their mobile phone will be smashed and legal and sharia punishment will be imposed on the violator.” It adds that any exemptions require a written decree from the Taliban supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada. The Guardian was unable to reach a Taliban spokesperson. related.title: Oil prices fall, stocks rally as US, Iran sign framework to end war
related.summary: Oil prices have dropped following the United States and Iran’s signing of an interim peace agreement, resuming a slide interrupted by US President Donald Trump’s warning that he could restart his military campaign. Sharif said Iran would “instantly reopen” the Strait of Hormuz and the US would “immediately” lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, though it was not immediately clear if the announcement had any effect on boosting maritime traffic in the critical waterway.
bullets: Oil prices have dropped following the United States and Iran’s signing of an interim peace agreement, resuming a slide interrupted by US President Donald Trump’s warning that he could restart his military campaign.

Sharif said Iran would “instantly reopen” the Strait of Hormuz and the US would “immediately” lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, though it was not immediately clear if the announcement had any effect on boosting maritime traffic in the critical waterway.
Shipping in the strait has been reduced to a fraction of peacetime levels due to the threat of Iranian missiles, drones and mines, as well as the US blockade.

In a statement earlier this week, the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO), one of the world’s largest associations for shipowners, said the US and Iran had yet to provide information about “key aspects such as timings and safe routes”.

“Putting aside the contents of the MoU, markets are likely to be welcoming the fact that both the US and Iran signed it sooner than initially expected,” Norihiro Yamaguchi, lead economist for Japan at Oxford Economics, told Al Jazeera.

related.title: Trump signs initial deal to end Iran war and open Strait of Hormuz as nuclear talks continue
related.summary: Much of the agreement would restore the status quo before the war, including ending hostilities, restarting talks between the US and Iran over Tehran’s nuclear project, and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial passage for the world’s oil and natural gas whose closure created a historic global energy crisis.
bullets: Much of the agreement would restore the status quo before the war, including ending hostilities, restarting talks between the US and Iran over Tehran’s nuclear project, and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial passage for the world’s oil and natural gas whose closure created a historic global energy crisis.

US President Donald Trump signed an agreement with Iran on Wednesday that calls for Tehran to dilute its stockpile of highly enriched uranium and waives US-backed sanctions on the country, immediately allowing Iran to sell its oil freely in a major concession from Washington, according to details released by both countries.

The agreement calls for a permanent end to hostilities and starts a 60-day negotiating clock to reach a final deal on the future of Iran's nuclear programme, though Trump left the door open to resume attacks.
